https://ianslive.in/president-murmu-retu.text: President Murmu returns to Delhi after concluding State visits to Moldova, North Macedonia, Romania IANS July 26, 2026 7:28 AM Share on | New Delhi, July 26 (IANS) President Droupadi Murmu returned to New Delhi on Sunday after successfully concluding her three-nation State visit to Moldova, North Macedonia and Romania, marking a significant diplomatic outreach aimed at strengthening India’s ties with the three European countries. Announcing her return, the official X handle of the President of India posted: “President Droupadi Murmu arrived in Delhi after completing her State visits to Moldova, North Macedonia and Romania.” During the final leg of the tour, President Murmu visited Romania, where she held wide-ranging talks with Romanian President Nicusor Dan on advancing bilateral cooperation and regional and global issues. According to the President’s Secretariat, President Murmu was warmly received by President Dan at the Cotroceni Palace in Bucharest and was accorded a ceremonial welcome and guard of honour. The two leaders held comprehensive discussions covering key aspects of the India-Romania partnership and also exchanged views on regional and global developments as well as multilateral cooperation. The visit also witnessed the signing of three Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) to expand bilateral collaboration in the fields of science and technology, sports, and the establishment of a Chair of Indian Studies at the University of Bucharest. President Murmu’s visit was historic as it marked the first State Visit by an Indian President to Romania in nearly three decades. She was accompanied by Minister of State for Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution Nimuben Jayantibhai Bambhaniya, along with Members of Parliament Dr. Dinesh Sharma and Vijay Baghel. Before arriving in Romania, President Murmu visited North Macedonia, the second stop of her three-nation tour, after concluding her engagements in Moldova. Upon her arrival in the capital, Skopje, she was welcomed by North Macedonia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, Timcho Mucunski. During the visit, President Murmu held discussions with President Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova and Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski, with the talks aimed at enhancing bilateral cooperation across multiple sectors and further deepening relations between the two countries. The President began her tour with a landmark visit to Moldova, becoming the first Indian President ever to visit the country. During her stay in Chisinau, she visited the Parliament of Moldova and met Speaker Igor Grosu along with members of the Parliamentary Friendship Group. According to the President’s Secretariat, President Murmu expressed confidence that the leaders of India and Moldova would continue working together to build a stronger, future-oriented and mutually beneficial partnership. She was welcomed on arrival at Chisinau International Airport by Moldova’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, Mihai Popșoi. --IANS rs/ LATEST NEWS ‘Three months of preparation yet thin crowd’: Rajbhar mocks Rahul’s event in Prayagraj August 8, 2026 Barcelona mourn passing of Jorge Messi, pay tribute to Lionel Messi’s father August 8, 2026 Brajesh Pathak, Sanjay Nishad slam Rahul’s event as 'flop show', defend double engine govt August 8, 2026 US Vice President Vance dials PM Modi, discusses strategic partnership August 8, 2026 'Healthy competition is motivating youngsters': Kanpur Superstars owner Lalwani on transformative impact of the UPT20 League August 8, 2026 Jimmy Neesham joins Glasgow Cosmic for inaugural edition of ETPL August 8, 2026 Pakistan cricketers return from unsanctioned Zambia league, face two-year PCB ban August 8, 2026 MoS Kirti Vardhan Singh calls on Cote d’Ivoire President, discusses growing partnership August 8, 2026 National Rural Livelihoods Mission aims to create women entrepreneurs in Kashmir August 8, 2026 Priyanka Chopra hops on the 'Kinda Chic” trend' August 8, 2026

https://www.dw.com/en/russian-students-p.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NE46 Patriotism has become a core part of the national curriculum since 2022 Image: Konstanin Kokoshkin/Pivcario/picture alliance Advertisement Earlier this year, several schools in Novosibirsk, a city of 1.6 million in southern Siberia, received a textbook on patriotism from the authorities. According to students, with whom DW spoke to on condition of anonymity, in the book the authors urge children to prepare themselves to die for their country. Furthermore, they equate homosexuality with pedophilia and Disney cartoons with pornography, and give instructions on how women should use their "charms." Europeans are described as "thieves, murderers and liars." The textbook, which provides "materials for spiritual, moral, and patriotic upbringing" is supposed to be used as part of "patriotism lessons" that have been on the curriculum since 2022 . Though it is not included on the national list of core curriculum books, the content reflects the Kremlin's intentions to spread propaganda in educational institutions. 'Love always involves sacrifice.' One of the main topics of the book is the war in Ukraine and the idea that dying for one's country is a blessing is repeated several times: "Love always involves sacrifice," writes one of the authors. "The sacrifice of a defender of the homeland is their life." Elsewhere in the book, the authors make constant claims that Russia is better than Western countries. They also say that children are "mentally crippled" because of "computer games, Hollywood action films, pornography and Disney cartoons." They argue that European nations that used to be colonial empires legitimized "murder, lies and plunder" through the conquest and subjugation of new territories. Russia, on the other hand, "never exploited its numerous peoples," they say, but merely improved their living conditions. The book makes no mention of the culture of Indigenous peoples in what is Russia today, or of any religions other than Christianity and "Slavic paganism." This textbook is used in certain Russian schools to teach children about patriotism and other subjects Image: M. Remaevich 'More cannon fodder' For Ilya, a 16-year-old student in Novosibirsk who has read the book and whose name has been changed, the idea of dying for his country is anathema. "It's proof that the country wants more cannon fodder," he told DW, adding that "dying for the country" actually meant dying for "the president's interests and ambitions." He said that a few years ago, he had started watching the videos of Alexei Navalny, the Kremlin critic and opposition leader who died in jail in 2024 "more for fun than for any other reason." He said it was Navalny's 2021 investigation into Russian President Vladimir Putin's Black Sea palace that had first drawn his attention. But it was when the authorities decided to block access to the US platforms YouTube and Discord that he began to oppose the government. He set up a VPN out of "contrariness" he said, looking for information about other opposition figures and reading the independent media. As he found out more about the cruelty and senselessness of the war, he criticized the government more strongly. He confirmed that propaganda had become an integral part of the curriculum in the past four years. On top of the "Conversations about Important Things" that take place every Monday morning, there are now also subjects such as "Fundamentals of Homeland Security and Defense." He said that people who have taken part in the war in Ukraine are invited to lessons focusing on students' future and decisions regarding what career path to take. Even outside of the classroom, students are encouraged to be "patriotic." Ilya said that a student had been reprimanded by the principal for wearing a sweater with a slogan written in English on it. "Young man, do you realize that your sweater has words on it in the language of unfriendly countries?" she reportedly asked him. "A call to the Federal Security Service will take care of that!" Ilya also recalled that a school assembly held to mark May 9, which commemorates the Soviet Union's victory over Nazi Germany in 1945, the principal and her deputy had compared what is known in Russia as the " Great Patriotic War " to the current war in Ukraine. They had said that Russia would once again be steadfast and emerge victorious. Students are taught about being a soldier and told it is an honor to die for the country Image: Konstantin Kokoshkin/Picvario/Russian Look/Global Look Press/picture alliance 'I love freedom' Alexei (name changed), another 16-year-old student in Novosibirsk, told DW that many of his classmates avoided going to "patriotic events." He too said that the blocking of YouTube had made a difference to him. "I looked into why it was blocked," he said. "Because nothing happens by chance. And that's how my interest in politics began." That's when he realized that the authorities wanted to get rid of inconvenient citizens and suppress free speech. "I love freedom, so it was hard," he said. Ilya thinks that most students don't take the propaganda seriously. "On the one hand, we laugh about it in class, at least my friends do," he said. "On the other, we don't care. Some simply don't listen. We're very good at being quiet and not talking much about it," Dima Zicer is an educator and the author of the Russian-language podcast "Love, Don't Discipline" who moved to Estonia after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine . He told DW that "many students are happy to be part of a pro-Putin majority that doesn't think about things, according to the principle: 'We'll crush them all; we're stronger than everyone else. Everyone will be scared of us.'" He said that there was no statistical data to back his argument, but he said that he had drawn his conclusions from his extensive experience working with Russian children, as well as his communication with parents. He said that these often only became aware of how serious the situation was when their children started saying things such as "We'll crush them" or "Putin is great," as well as talking about supposed Nazis and fascists in Ukraine. Alexei and Ilya, who think differently and want the war in Ukraine to end, are worried about the unstable situation in Russia. They want to leave the country after graduating. https://www.wdiy.org/npr-news/2026-10-04.text: On Air Now Playing WDIY NPR News She died covering war for Fox News. Her parents blame the network — and a star reporter NPR | By David Folkenflik Published October 4, 2026 at 6:00 AM EDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Print Listen • 35:15 AFP via Getty Images, Paula Bronstein for NPR and family photos / Collage by Mark Harris for NPR Updated October 5, 2026 at 7:07 PM EDT 🎧 Prefer to listen to this story? Hear it in the NPR app . NPR Ukraine producers Polina Lytvynova and Hanna Palamarenko contributed to this story. When the Fox News Channel hosted hundreds of advertisers and industry executives at the ornate Hammerstein Ballroom in Manhattan two years ago, the network centered attention on a tragic yet heroic figure: the war correspondent Benjamin Hall. "From Ukraine to the Middle East, and here at home, the dedicated journalists of Fox News are trying to inform Americans, even in the most perilous of circumstances," Hall proclaimed . Fox News / Screenshot by NPR Fox News correspondent Benjamin Hall is treated for injuries that he sustained while reporting in Ukraine in March 2022. Hall knows peril all too well. In the first weeks of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, a strike by Russian forces hit the car in which Hall's team had been traveling outside Kyiv. Hall had nearly died. He lost his right leg below the knee, most of his left foot and part of an eye. Two years after the attack, Hall stood center stage on prostheses, in a suit that ended just above his knees. He entered to a standing ovation. Seth Wenig / AP Hall is interviewed about his book, Saved: A War Reporter's Mission to Make It Home , on Fox & Friends on March 10, 2023. "These stories, they need eyes on the ground," Hall said. "They need a human perspective. They need us to bear witness." But at what cost? Though gravely injured, Hall was the lucky one. The strike killed all four people who traveled with Hall that day: The two Ukrainian soldiers who served as guides. Pierre Zakrzewski, a beloved Fox war videographer. And Oleksandra Kuvshynova, known as Sasha. The 24-year-old Ukrainian had just joined the team as a producer and interpreter. Fox News / Screenshot by NPR Oleksandra "Sasha" Kuvshynova and Pierre Zakrzewski. Fox has described the deaths as tragic and honored the fallen. Yet two multimillion-dollar lawsuits against the network blame it for what happened. One of those lawsuits has been filed by Kuvshynova's parents, who also squarely blame Hall. In their first joint interview about the tragedy, they tell NPR they are speaking out to honor their daughter's life and document what they contend is the injustice of her death. Paula Bronstein for NPR / Andriy Kuvshynov and Iryna Mamaysur hold a portrait of their daughter, Oleksandra Kuvshynova, in 2024. Two high-risk security advisers who worked for Fox News in Ukraine bolster the family's claims. In separate interviews with NPR about what happened, they say Fox News and its star correspondent ignored repeated and urgent warnings to stay away from the danger zone outside the city limits of Kyiv. "If you took Benji out of the equation, this never would have happened," Aaron King, one of those security advisers, said. The other adviser, Shane Thomson, has joined the Kuvshynovs' lawsuit, alleging Fox scapegoated him for the tragedy. This story is based on 15 interviews and a review of hundreds of pages of legal documents, as well as Fox's own broadcasts. Fox News, citing the ongoing litigation, declined NPR's repeated and detailed requests for interviews with Fox officials, news executives and lawyers before this story's publication. The network also did not make Hall available for interviews for this story. It additionally declined to respond to specific questions raised for this story. After this story's publication, Fox News issued this statement: "Ben Hall was a victim of this brutal war zone attack and the lawsuit's attempt to shift blame onto him is deeply shameful." Sam McQueen for NPR / Shane Thomson was a high-risk security contractor for Fox News during the beginning of the war in Ukraine. He has joined a lawsuit against the network. One of the most revealing witnesses to Hall's character is Hall himself. He wrote a memoir, published a year after the attack, in which he acknowledged increasingly embracing risk as his career and ambitions progressed. The same year, he also presented his story in a Fox documentary. Fox and its founder, Rupert Murdoch, have faced controversies, scandals and litigation before. Often, accusations center on the network's right-wing ideology, Murdoch's own political agenda or their relentless pursuit of profits. This is different. Two words define the underlying allegations in the Kuvshynovs' wrongful death lawsuit against Fox and Hall: ambition and negligence. Fox calls the deaths tragic but rejects responsibility Covering any armed conflict by definition involves peril. Hazards are often ambiguous; the boundaries of battle zones are fluid. Combat journalists for many news organizations, including NPR , have been killed. But the Kuvshynovs and their legal team say what happened to their daughter was preventable — and foreseen. "This was a very avoidable danger that they were specifically warned about, as to [the] exact time and place that they could not go," charges Stephen Humphreys, a lawyer for the Kuvshynovs and Thomson. Paula Bronstein for NPR / American lawyer Stephen Humphreys is representing Kuvshynova's parents in their lawsuit against Fox News. He is seen in Kyiv, Ukraine, in 2024. In court statements in the Kuvshynovs' suit, Fox acknowledges the tragedy of the deaths of Kuvshynova and Zakrzewski. But the network counters the plaintiffs' claims on technical and legal grounds. In declining comment for this story, Fox pointed NPR to a statement released in March 2024, when the lawsuit was filed. "While we understand the grief and continue to mourn the loss of both Pierre Zakrzewski and Sasha Kuvshynova, we will respectfully defend against the inaccurate claims within this lawsuit," Fox said. "The safety of our journalists has always been our number one priority and we are immensely grateful to the Fox News journalists who have covered the war in Ukraine and we remain committed to reporting from the region," the statement continues. Hall: "I learned that I could control my fear" AFP via Getty Images and family photos / Collage by Mark Harris for NPR It wasn't clear that Hall would get to Kyiv in early 2022. A dual British-U.S. citizen, Hall was inspired by his globe-trotting family's past. He wrote in his memoir that at the outset of World War II, his dad's family was in the Philippines. Japanese forces took Hall's grandfather prisoner and executed his grandmother and other relatives. U.S. troops rescued Hall's father, then just a boy. In chronicling combat, Hall wrote, "I saw a lot of death, had guns pressed against my head, dreamed horrific dreams — all of it an echo of what my father endured in Manila." In his 20s, Hall pinged from one hot spot to another, freelancing for outlets like Vice and Esquire , and Fox. The first time Hall saw a man die was in Misrata, Libya, in 2011. He had a choice, he recounted in the memoir, titled Saved : He could turn away or, perhaps, "invade the dignity of those moments in order to 'get the story.'" "I did not have the time to consider all the moral angles. I could either keep filming, or stop filming, and I chose to keep filming," Hall wrote. He added that he had just escaped being killed too. Paul Morigi / Getty Images Fox News correspondent Trey Yingst attends the 2026 White House Correspondents' Dinner on April 25. Back in London, Hall registered that he had undergone a profound transformation. "I learned that I could control my fear, even bury it, and keep moving forward into danger," Hall wrote. "I learned that the hellishness of Misrata was not enough to stop me from going to combat zones. "And I learned that my normal civilized life would never be the same again. No — this was who I was now." Years later, his colleague Trey Yingst would call Hall "the gold standard" for war zone reporting for the network. But there was at least one early red flag. In a sworn affidavit for the Kuvshynovs' lawsuit, former Fox News international producer Phil Ittner said he had previously lodged a formal internal complaint that Hall's behavior in Syria had placed colleagues in danger. "Ben Hall was addicted to the adrenaline rush of taking risks," Ittner wrote in the affidavit. "I worried that he put his career promotion ahead of the safety of the crew working with him." He called for Hall to be pulled from the field. Instead, Ittner wrote in the affidavit, Fox never responded. No known consequences ensued. (In its legal filings, Fox responded that Ittner has no knowledge of events in Ukraine as he had been forced out of the network three years earlier.) In 2015, Hall promised his girlfriend, Alicia Meller, that he would find a safer path as they started a family. They soon married. He also took a full-time job in Fox's London bureau, which still entailed covering conflict and strife. But in 2021, Hall moved to Washington, D.C., to cover the U.S. State Department. Tasos Katopodis / Getty Images Benjamin Hall hosts Fox News Sunday on May 12, 2024. "I made that final decision to pull back from the front lines," Hall wrote. "It was much harder than I imagined it would be to make this professional change in my life; the pull of distant wars never weakened or went away. But I understood new paths were opening for me." That new path lasted roughly four months. On Feb. 24, 2022, Russian President Vladimir Putin announced the invasion of Ukraine. Hall got a call from a Fox News executive: Would he go overseas and cover the war? As he wrote, "I understood my obligations to Alicia and my family, and I knew I had to stop putting myself in dangerous situations." Still, off he went. From D.C. to Lviv Four days after the Russians invaded, Hall arrived in the city of Lviv. It was an arduous drive from Poland; he was swimming against the tide as long columns of motorists were fleeing Ukraine. He started reporting and hosting a show that aired nightly on Fox. The major action, however, was hundreds of miles to the east. Fox had established news coverage from Kyiv with a team of journalists; now it was pulling producers out as the risk increased. Only a skeleton crew remained. Aris Messinis / AFP via Getty Images Firefighters put out a fire after a bombing of the eastern Ukrainian town of Chuhuiv on Feb. 24, 2022, as Russian armed forces invaded Ukraine. Yet Fox summoned all its journalists in Lviv for a Zoom call, Hall wrote in Saved . Executives hoped to send another correspondent to Kyiv. "All of us wanted to go, including me," Hall wrote. He was the one invited. Hall's wife urged him not to go, he wrote. He assured her he'd be fine. Fox had a team of high-risk security contractors to keep its journalists safe. Such security advisers typically have military backgrounds. They provide guidance, muscle and medical aid. They can also serve as a brake on journalists who put their hunger for a story ahead of their own well-being. Aaron King was one of Fox's high-risk security advisers. He says that like Hall's wife — and like another Fox safety contractor — he told Hall not to go to Kyiv. "It wasn't in his best interest to go down there," King said. "And I asked him what he believed that he would achieve that other teams haven't already achieved at this point in time." King says it was like all battle zone assignments — balancing the risks versus the possible reward. "He kind of processed what I'd spoken to him about, for about 10 seconds, kind of shrugged his shoulders and said, 'Ah, I'll go anyway,'" King said. "And that was the last I seen of Benjamin." In his book, Hall presented the pull to Kyiv as inescapable. "I could not say no to the offer to go to Kyiv and continue anchoring the show from there," he wrote in Saved . "It was, in a way, the culmination of all that I had worked on and all the risks I'd taken before. It was the big one, the war that might change the world—change the course of history. This was who I was and what I had prepared to do." Sasha Kuvshynova: A life filled with promise Kuvshynov family / Kuvshynova in 2021. Among the people Hall would encounter once he arrived in Kyiv was Sasha Kuvshynova, Fox's new Gen Z fixer. Her Facebook page bears a motto in English: "if you never try you will never know." Her other social media accounts brim with life too: music and film festivals, her photographic shoots, travel to Tuscany , pictures of her as a child , her cat, Zephyr. She posted about her pride that her father , trained as a physicist, taught her math. Her accounts turned grim starting in February 2022, after the invasion by Russia. After a Russian strike on the primary television tower in Kyiv, she posted on Instagram : "Glory to Ukraine!" Kuvshynova's mother, Iryna Mamaysur, and her father, Andriy Kuvshynov, spoke with pride laced with sorrow during hourslong interviews by video conference from NPR's Kyiv bureau, sometimes interrupted by air raid sirens. Their words were interpreted by two NPR Ukrainian producers present. Kuvshynova's parents say she was remarkable from her youngest years. (Under Ukrainian naming conventions, Kuvshynova took the surname of her father, with an added "a" to reflect her gender.) She learned to read by 3, mastered English by 11 and showed flair as an interpreter early on, her mother said. As a teen, Kuvshynova briefly aided foreign reporters during the popular uprising in 2014 against Ukraine's then pro-Russian president, who ultimately fled. That's when she met Zakrzewski, the Fox video journalist, and discovered how to blend her interests into a single passion: to tell Ukraine's story. When Fox approached her in early 2022 to aid its reporting on the coming war, she embraced the offer eagerly. "I will tell you that I was very glad," her father said. "I thought that getting into such a level of a global, vital company [would be a good experience]. Fascinating material, interesting people." "She was excited," her mother recalled. "She said, 'I have already found my profession.'" From Lviv to Kyiv Aris Messinis / AFP via Getty Images Sergyi Badylevych kisses his young child as his wife, Natalia Badylevych, stands nearby in an underground metro station used as bomb shelter in Kyiv on March 2, 2022. Hall arrived in the Ukrainian capital on March 2. The Fox crew stayed at the InterContinental Kyiv, a luxury hotel in the historical heart of the Ukrainian capital. Other networks holed up there too. He encountered the familiar faces of Yingst and Zakrzewski, a crackerjack visual journalist with a big heart, a mischievous streak and a salt-and-pepper walrus mustache. Kuvshynova had also moved into the hotel. As a "fixer" for Fox, she was in touch with people in the Ukrainian military and the government and scouted possible sites and scenes to film. She knew the language, and she knew her way around. It was home. Kuvshynova would send her parents reassuring texts frequently. She let them know, for example, when she had returned from outings near battle zones. "She said, 'Mom, don't worry. We have security on these crews who are very experienced,'" said her mother, Iryna Mamaysur. And she joked, given the protective gear they all wore, that she was "a very fashionable lady who outfits our team." Toward the end of each day, the team would hold what it called "evening prayers," based on a British military practice. The crew would break down its intentions for the next day and map out the logistics with Fox producers and security consultants. Senior producers in London and Jerusalem and even executives in New York City would participate in the call. A senior network executive or security official was supposed to sign off on each assignment, particularly if it involved going
